questions.question: 1. What is the best-case time complexity of Quick Sort when each partition divides the array into two approximately equal parts?

explanations.a: Correct. With balanced partitions, there are approximately $\log_2(n)$ levels of recursion, and each level performs $O(n)$ total partitioning work, giving $O(n \log n)$ time.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Quadratic time results from repeatedly highly unbalanced partitions, not approximately equal partitions.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Each recursion level requires partitioning work across the elements, so the total is greater than linear when multiple levels are required.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The recursion depth can be logarithmic, but partitioning work at each level also contributes to the total running time.

questions.question: 2. What is the average-case time complexity of Quick Sort when the pivot selection usually produces reasonably balanced partitions?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Quadratic time is associated with repeatedly highly unbalanced partitions and represents the worst-case behavior.
explanations.b: Correct. Reasonably balanced partitions lead to about $\log_2(n)$ recursion levels, with $O(n)$ partitioning work per level, giving average-case time $O(n \log n)$.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Quick Sort generally requires several partitioning levels, so the total work is greater than linear.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The logarithmic quantity describes the approximate recursion depth for balanced partitions, not the total running time.

questions.question: 3. Which situation produces the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort?

answers.a: The pivot repeatedly divides the array into nearly equal parts.
answers.b: The pivot is selected randomly and produces balanced partitions most of the time.
answers.c: The pivot repeatedly produces one very small partition and one partition containing almost all remaining elements.
answers.d: The array contains elements that are all distinct.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Nearly equal partitions reduce the problem size substantially at each recursion level.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Balanced partitions generally lead to efficient average-case behavior.
explanations.c: Correct. Repeatedly producing highly unbalanced partitions creates nearly linear recursion depth and results in $O(n^2)$ time.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Having distinct elements does not by itself determine whether the partitions will be balanced or unbalanced.

questions.question: 4. Consider the recurrence $T(n) = 2T(n / 2) + O(n)$ for Quick Sort. What time complexity does this recurrence represent?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The recursive subproblems create multiple levels of work, so the total is greater than linear.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Quadratic time corresponds to highly unbalanced recursion rather than two approximately half-sized recursive subproblems.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The logarithmic quantity describes the recursion depth, but each level also performs linear partitioning work.
explanations.d: Correct. The recurrence has two subproblems of size approximately $n / 2$ and $O(n)$ partitioning work at each level, resulting in $O(n \log n)$ time.

questions.question: 5. In the worst case, Quick Sort can be represented by the recurrence $T(n) = T(n - 1) + O(n)$. What is the resulting time complexity?

explanations.a: Correct. The recurrence performs partitioning work on subarrays of sizes approximately $n, n - 1, n - 2, \ldots$, giving a total proportional to $n^2$.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This would describe a much more balanced recursion pattern than the one represented by the recurrence.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The partitioning work is repeated across many decreasing subarray sizes, so it exceeds linear time.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The recursion depth is linear in this worst-case pattern, not logarithmic.

questions.question: 6. What is the typical auxiliary space complexity of recursive Quick Sort when the partitions are reasonably balanced?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The recursion stack does not grow quadratically with the input size.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Linear auxiliary stack space is associated with highly unbalanced recursion rather than balanced recursion.
explanations.c: Correct. Balanced recursion has a depth of approximately $\log_2(n)$, so the recursive call stack typically requires $O(\log n)$ auxiliary space.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Recursive calls require stack frames, so the auxiliary space is not always constant.

questions.question: 7. In the worst case, what can happen to the auxiliary space used by recursive Quick Sort?

answers.a: It becomes $O(\log n)$ regardless of the pivot selection.
answers.b: It can become $O(n)$ because the recursion depth can become linear.
answers.c: It becomes $O(n^2)$ because every comparison creates a stack frame.
answers.d: It becomes $O(1)$ because Quick Sort is always in-place.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Logarithmic recursion depth depends on balanced partitioning and is not guaranteed for every pivot selection.
explanations.b: Correct. Repeatedly highly unbalanced partitions can produce recursion depth proportional to $n$, requiring $O(n)$ stack space.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A stack frame is associated with an active recursive call, not with every individual comparison.
explanations.d: Incorrect. In-place partitioning reduces array-storage requirements but does not eliminate recursive call-stack space.

questions.question: 8. Which statement correctly compares Quick Sort with Merge Sort and Heap Sort in terms of standard time complexity?

answers.a: Quick Sort has $O(n \log n)$ worst-case time, while Merge Sort has $O(n^2)$ worst-case time.
answers.b: Quick Sort has $O(n)$ average-case time, while Heap Sort has $O(\log n)$ worst-case time.
answers.c: Quick Sort has $O(n \log n)$ average-case time but $O(n^2)$ worst-case time, while Merge Sort and Heap Sort have $O(n \log n)$ worst-case time.
answers.d: All three algorithms have $O(n)$ worst-case time.

explanations.a: Incorrect. The stated worst-case complexities for Quick Sort and Merge Sort are not correct.
explanations.b: Incorrect. These bounds are too low to represent the standard sorting complexities of the algorithms mentioned.
explanations.c: Correct. Quick Sort typically has $O(n \log n)$ average-case time but can reach $O(n^2)$ in the worst case, whereas Merge Sort and Heap Sort have $O(n \log n)$ worst-case time.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Sorting an arbitrary array cannot generally be accomplished in linear worst-case time by these comparison-based algorithms.

questions.question: 9. Why does Quick Sort have $O(n \log n)$ time when its partitions are balanced?

answers.a: There are approximately $\log_2(n)$ partitioning levels, and the total partitioning work across each level is $O(n)$.
answers.b: There are $n$ partitioning levels, and each level performs constant work.
answers.c: The algorithm performs only $\log_2(n)$ comparisons in total.
answers.d: The algorithm does not need to process every element during partitioning.

explanations.a: Correct. Balanced partitioning reduces the subarray size by roughly half at each level, giving about $\log_2(n)$ levels, while each level performs a total of $O(n)$ partitioning work.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Balanced recursion does not create $n$ levels; the number of levels grows logarithmically.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Quick Sort performs many more than $\log_2(n)$ comparisons over the entire execution.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The partitioning process must examine the elements in the current subarray to place them on the appropriate side of the pivot.
